sumifs-per-region.code:
SELECT region,
       SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM sales
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY region;
sumifs-per-region.explanation: The formula is filled down for each region, so in SQL it becomes one query that groups the sales by region and adds the amounts from 1 January 2026 onwards.

mapping.note: One row per region instead of one formula per row.
The date condition applies to every group.

assumptions: Regions that have no sales in 2026 do not appear; the spreadsheet would show 0 for them.
Rows with an empty amount (NULL) are ignored by SUM, like blank cells in SUMIFS.

countifs-no-schema.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS open_high_priority
FROM tickets
WHERE status = 'Open'
  AND priority > 5;
countifs-no-schema.explanation: COUNTIFS counts the rows that meet both conditions; SQL counts the rows that pass the WHERE clause.

mapping.note: Column C assumed to be status.
Column D assumed to be priority.

assumptions: The sheet Tickets is a table called tickets.
Column C is status and column D is priority (a number).
MySQL compares text without regard to case with the default collation, like COUNTIFS.

vlookup-left-join.code:
SELECT o.id,
       o.product_code,
       p.price
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN products AS p
  ON p.code = o.product_code;
vlookup-left-join.explanation: An exact-match VLOOKUP becomes a LEFT JOIN: every order row keeps its place, and orders whose code is missing from products get NULL, like #N/A.

mapping.target: LEFT JOIN products ON p.code = o.product_code
mapping.note: B2 is the product code of the order row.
The third column of the lookup range.

assumptions: Product codes are unique in products; duplicates would repeat order rows, while VLOOKUP returns only the first match.

xlookup-pandas-merge.code:
import pandas as pd

# orders and customers are DataFrames loaded from your data
result = orders.merge(
    customers[["id", "email"]],
    how="left",
    left_on="customer_id",
    right_on="id",
)
result["email"] = result["email"].fillna("Not found")
result = result.drop(columns=["id"])
xlookup-pandas-merge.explanation: XLOOKUP becomes a left merge on the customer ID; fillna supplies the "Not found" value for IDs that are missing.

mapping.note: Column C assumed to be email.

assumptions: Column C of Customers holds the email.
Customer IDs are unique in customers.

if-chain-case-when.code:
SELECT student,
       score,
       CASE
           WHEN score >= 90 THEN 'A'
           WHEN score >= 75 THEN 'B'
           WHEN score >= 60 THEN 'C'
           ELSE 'F'
       END AS grade
FROM results;
if-chain-case-when.explanation: Each nested IF becomes one WHEN branch, tested in the same order; ELSE is the last IF's value_if_false.
assumptions: A NULL score gets F; in the spreadsheet an empty cell counts as 0 and also gets F.

if-chain-np-select.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

conditions = [
    df["score"] >= 90,
    df["score"] >= 75,
    df["score"] >= 60,
]
choices = ["A", "B", "C"]
df["grade"] = np.select(conditions, choices, default="F")
if-chain-np-select.explanation: np.select takes the conditions in order and uses the first one that is true, like nested IF; default is the final value_if_false.
assumptions: Missing scores (NaN) get F, because NaN >= 90 is False.

sumproduct-conditions.code:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'North' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS north_amount
FROM sales;
sumproduct-conditions.explanation: SUMPRODUCT multiplies a TRUE/FALSE test by the amounts; SQL adds the amount only when the condition is true.
assumptions: PostgreSQL compares text case-sensitively; the spreadsheet does not. Use LOWER(region) = 'north' if the case varies.
warnings: String comparison is case-sensitive in PostgreSQL but not in the spreadsheet.

running-total-window.code:
SELECT paid_on,
       amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY paid_on ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM payments
ORDER BY paid_on;
running-total-window.explanation: A growing range $C$2:C2 is a running total; a window function adds every row up to the current one in date order.
assumptions: Rows on the same date are added in the order the database reads them, as ROWS is used.

approximate-vlookup.code:
SELECT p.id,
       p.weight,
       (SELECT r.price
          FROM rates AS r
         WHERE r.min_weight <= p.weight
         ORDER BY r.min_weight DESC
         LIMIT 1) AS price
FROM parcels AS p;
approximate-vlookup.explanation: Approximate-match VLOOKUP finds the largest limit that is not above the weight. A plain join cannot do that, so a subquery picks the row with the highest min_weight <= weight (the same as MAX of the matching limits).

mapping.target: correlated subquery ORDER BY min_weight DESC LIMIT 1

assumptions: Weights below the smallest limit get NULL, like #N/A in the spreadsheet.
warnings: Approximate-match VLOOKUP has no direct JOIN equivalent; the subquery reproduces it.

injection-in-source.code:
SELECT SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM invoices;
injection-in-source.explanation: SUM over a column range becomes SUM over the column.

mapping.note: Column B assumed to be amount.

assumptions: Column B is the amount column of invoices; every row is included, not only rows 2 to 50.

injection-in-schema.code:
SELECT AVG(score) AS average_score
FROM scores;
injection-in-schema.explanation: AVERAGE becomes AVG; both skip empty cells / NULL.
assumptions: SQLite returns a decimal average even though score is an integer column.
